Player-1: Learning to Play from
Synthetic Experience

Mingyu Ouyang, Yiran Wang, Siyuan Hu, Xingyilang Yin, Huiqiang Sun, Guangzhi Wang, Junfu Pu, Cheng Cheng, Honghao Chen, Ying Shan, Mike Zheng Shou, Hwee Tou Ng
National University of Singapore ARC Lab, Tencent IEG Nanyang Technological University
Abstract

Computer-use agents have demonstrated strong capabilities in interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions. However, games, with their visually rich worlds and diverse mechanics, remain challenging and offer a demanding next step toward general digital control. Current game-agent learning pipelines often rely on large-scale demonstrations with limited coverage of dynamic game states, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. We introduce Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. For supervised initialization, we fine-tune computer-use models on 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories that pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning. We construct Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with PPO. The resulting Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B improve MineDojo-300 success over their SFT policies by 27.8 and 17.7 percentage points, respectively. Player-1-9B reaches 38.33% success compared with 12.63% for the strongest evaluated baseline, with further gains over SFT on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld. Further analyses show that broader synthetic environment coverage improves transfer, while the use of composite actions that combine multiple keyboard and mouse inputs increases during RL. We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience substantially improves game control beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

1 Introduction

Foundation models have developed broad capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and instruction following (OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025; Gemini Team, 2025). Computer-use agents bring these capabilities to digital interfaces, interpreting screens and executing keyboard and mouse actions (Wang et al., 2025a; Bai et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2026). Games offer a demanding next step toward general digital control: their visually complex environments and diverse mechanics require precise, sustained, and concurrent control under dynamic and rapidly changing visual feedback (Luo et al., 2026a).

Recent game agents learn from large-scale gameplay demonstrations and interactive experience (Wang et al., 2025b; Magne et al., 2026; SIMA Team, 2025; Shi et al., 2026). Yet demonstrations cover only a limited portion of the states an agent may encounter in open-ended tasks, while scalable environments for interactive training remain difficult to obtain. Despite differences in appearance and rules, we find that many games share recurring control demands such as precise aiming, sustained movement, and coordinated inputs. This motivates our central question: Can synthetic experience advance game-control capabilities beyond supervised initialization, with gains that generalize to games outside the RL training suite?

Three challenges shape this approach. First, gameplay demonstrations recorded with heterogeneous input conventions and temporal resolutions must be converted into a shared action space, and paired with task instructions and visual reasoning that reflect the player’s intent. Second, learning beyond demonstrations requires feedback on states reached by the policy’s own actions, but implementing programmatic rewards across diverse commercial games is difficult to scale. Third, experience from environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales must be incorporated into a shared policy that generalizes beyond the training suite. These challenges motivate our supervised initialization from curated demonstrations, followed by learning in controllable synthetic environments with verifiable rewards.

We present Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience, as illustrated in Figure 1. We extend the computer-use action space with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions. Curated gameplay demonstrations pair recorded actions with task instructions and visual reasoning to initialize game control. Player-1-Gym then provides sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around recurring control demands across aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction. Programmatic game-state rewards and randomization of observations and control dynamics support multi-environment reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), yielding Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B. Table 1 summarizes the differences and focuses of representative game-agent learning pipelines.

Our results demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience improves game-control capabilities, with gains extending beyond the RL training suite. On MineDojo-300, Player-1-9B improves from 10.54% success after SFT to 38.33%, exceeding the strongest evaluated external baseline at 12.63% under our evaluation protocol. The same policy also improves on ViZDoom-10 and GameWorld, both outside the RL training suite. We summarize our main contributions as follows:

  • •

    We present Player-1, a post-training framework that builds on supervised initialization to learn transferable game-control capabilities from synthetic experience. A shared action space supports relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions, while 6,044 curated gameplay trajectories provide supervised initialization for subsequent interactive learning.

  • •

    We introduce Player-1-Gym, sixteen synthetic 2D and 3D environments designed around recurring control demands across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, provide diverse experience for multi-environment reinforcement learning beyond demonstrations.

  • •

    We demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond supervised demonstrations: Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B gain 27.8 and 17.7 pp in MineDojo-300 success, respectively, with further gains on ViZDoom and GameWorld outside the RL training suite. Further analyses show improved transfer with broader environment coverage and increased composite-action use during RL.

2 Related Work

Generalist and Computer-Use Agents.

Foundation models provide broad language, reasoning, and multimodal capabilities that underpin general-purpose agents (OpenAI, 2024; Anthropic, 2025; Gemini Team, 2025; Yang et al., 2025). Vision-language models (VLMs) connect visual perception with language, supporting scene understanding and spatial grounding (Bai et al., 2025). Computer-use agents (CUAs) specialize these capabilities for screenshot-conditioned interaction, using keyboard and mouse actions to complete multi-step tasks (Hu et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025a; Lu et al., 2026).

Game Agents, Development, and Environments.

Game-agent research spans planning-based systems (Tan et al., 2025b), learned visual policies and vision–language–action (VLA) models (SIMA Team, 2024; Tan et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Magne et al., 2026; Yue et al., 2026), and joint video–action models (Guo et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning further supports self-improvement and long-horizon control (SIMA Team, 2025; Shi et al., 2026). Most recently, Jev demonstrates low-latency game control through a text-only interface, relying on structured game-state representations rather than screenshot observations (Almeida, 2026). Complementary benchmarks evaluate gameplay (Ouyang et al., 2026) and agentic game development (Chi et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026b). Code world models synthesized from rules and trajectories support planning (Lehrach et al., 2026), while game engine development provides trajectory data for world-model training (Zhou et al., 2026), connecting game creation to learning (Luo et al., 2026a).

Agent Post-Training with Verifiable Rewards.

Post-training with verifiable rewards enables agents to learn from the outcomes of their own actions. Environment-synthesis approaches expand training coverage by constructing interactive tasks with verifiable rewards (Dong et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a). Adaptive approaches learn which environments to generate or jointly improve the policy, environment, and reward model (Liu et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b). In games, SIMA 2 combines supervised initialization with online RLVR and further demonstrates self-improvement transfer across Genie 3 environments (SIMA Team, 2025). Player-1 combines supervised initialization with learning from synthetic experience in environments organized around shared control demands, demonstrating game-control gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite.

3 Method

Player-1 connects supervised initialization with learning from synthetic experience through a shared game-control action space. We first extend computer-use actions to support dynamic game control, and initialize the policy using curated gameplay demonstrations. We then optimize the policy across Player-1-Gym’s synthetic environments using PPO with verifiable rewards.

3.1 Extending the Computer-Use Action Space

We extend the computer-use action space for dynamic game control while retaining screenshot-conditioned decision making. At turn tt, the policy receives task instruction qq, screenshot ItI_{t}, and interaction history CH​(h<t)C_{H}(h_{<t}) (see Section 3.2):

(zt,a^t)∼πθ(⋅∣q,It,CH(h<t)).(z_{t},\hat{a}_{t})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid q,I_{t},C_{H}(h_{<t})).

Here ztz_{t} is reasoning and a^t\hat{a}_{t} the proposed action. The game-control action space extends the base model’s computer-use actions with relative pointer motion, sustained inputs, and composite actions.

Relative pointer motion.

For the mouse actions, CUAs typically use normalized absolute coordinates to select visible targets by specifying their on-screen positions. In game-play scenarios, to control the camera without a visible pointer, we extend this action space with relative displacements:

𝒜pointer={absolute⁡(x,y)}⏟Retained CUA coordinates∪{𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞⁡(𝚫​𝒙,𝚫​𝒚)}⏟Relative-motion extension.\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{pointer}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{absolute}(x,y)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA coordinates}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{relative}(\Delta x,\Delta y)\}}}_{\textbf{Relative-motion extension}}.

Absolute coordinates satisfy x,y∈[0,1000]x,y\in[0,1000], while relative displacements Δ​x,Δ​y∈[−1000,1000]\Delta x,\Delta y\in[-1000,1000] are normalized by screen width and height. Positive Δ​x\Delta x denotes rightward motion, and positive Δ​y\Delta y denotes downward motion. The resulting view rotation depends on the game’s camera gain.

Sustained inputs.

We extend taps and clicks with holds lasting one full control step of duration Δ​t\Delta t. For a key or mouse button bb, the press or long-hold action space is

𝒜press​(b)={tap/click⁡(b)}⏟Retained CUA taps/clicks∪{𝐡𝐨𝐥𝐝⁡(𝒃,𝚫​𝒕)}⏟Sustained extension.\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{press}}(b)=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{tap/click}(b)\}}_{\text{Retained CUA taps/clicks}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\operatorname{hold}(b;\Delta t)\}}}_{\textbf{Sustained extension}}.

Repeating holds across consecutive control steps sustains movement and interaction.

Composite actions.

We define a composite action as two or more compatible keyboard or mouse inputs executed concurrently within one control step. The step action space is

𝒜step={wait}∪𝒜keyboard∪𝒜mouse⏟Individual CUA inputs∪{input𝟏∥⋯∥input𝒎}⏟Composite-action extension.\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{step}}=\underbrace{\{\operatorname{wait}\}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}}_{\text{Individual CUA inputs}}\;\cup\;\underbrace{\boldsymbol{\{\textbf{input}_{1}\parallel\cdots\parallel\textbf{input}_{m}\}}}_{\textbf{Composite-action extension}}.

Each inputi∈𝒜keyboard∪𝒜mouse\text{input}_{i}\in\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{keyboard}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{mouse}}; ∥\parallel denotes concurrent execution and m≥2m\geq 2. These combinations support coordinated movement and combat that is crucial for game control. For example, holding ‘W’ while tapping ‘Space’ enables running jumps, and pointer motion with a right-button hold and left-button click enables concurrent aiming and firing.

3.2 Supervised Initialization for Game Control

The extended action space in Section 3.1 defines the available controls, but the policy must learn when and how to use them. In this section, we describe how we use SFT on a compact collection of curated gameplay demonstrations to initialize computer-use models for subsequent learning from synthetic experience.

Demonstration trajectory curation.

We curate 6,044 gameplay trajectories comprising 295,097 interaction turns from public datasets (Choi et al., 2026; Markov AI, 2026; Yue et al., 2026; Baker et al., 2022) and in-house recordings, mapping recorded controls to the shared game-control action space defined in Section 3.1. Controls are aligned to shared action intervals, and source-specific mouse calibration expresses relative inputs in normalized, pixel-equivalent coordinates. After filtering incomplete or redundant recordings, we use a VLM (Google DeepMind, 2026) to annotate the recorded actions with task instructions and per-turn visual reasoning. For reasoning annotation, the VLM conditions on the task instruction, current and past observations, and the action target. Figure 2 illustrates input coverage and an annotated demonstration. Appendix B details the sources, alignment, calibration, and annotation procedures.

Supervised fine-tuning.

We construct each SFT example as (q,It,CH​(h<t),zt,at)(q,I_{t},C_{H}(h_{<t}),z_{t},a_{t}), where the task instruction qq, current screenshot ItI_{t}, and retained history CH​(h<t)C_{H}(h_{<t}) form the policy input, while visual reasoning ztz_{t} and action ata_{t} provide supervision. Following Wang et al. (2025b), our SFT, RL, and evaluation share a 2+22+2 history setting: two recent visual–action turns and two earlier action-only turns, with reasoning omitted. We fine-tune the policy to predict (zt,at)(z_{t},a_{t}) conditioned on the task instruction, current screenshot, and retained history. We use action-balanced sampling detailed in Appendix D.1 to increase exposure to less frequent controls and composite actions.

3.3 Player-1-Gym: Learning from Synthetic Experience

We construct Player-1-Gym, a suite of synthetic environments organized around control demands shared across games. Programmatically verifiable rewards, together with randomized observations and control dynamics, support our multi-environment PPO training of the SFT-initialized policy.

Verifiable environment construction.

We identify recurring control demands across games and organize training tasks into five families: aiming, combat, driving, navigation, and UI interaction. For example, aiming tasks require pointer-based or camera-relative target tracking, while combat tasks combine movement with attack timing. Building upon our own shared 2D and 3D engines, reusable assets, and scene templates, we implement sixteen environments that require these forms of control through different game mechanics, viewpoints, and spatial layouts, as shown in Figure 3(a–b). A unified runtime provides screenshot observations and executes the shared game-control action space. This shared foundation facilitates extending the suite with new environments while maintaining consistent observation and action interfaces.

To provide verifiable training feedback, each environment defines game- and task-specific scoring rules over changing game states. Score increments supply step-level rewards, providing dense and verifiable feedback without a learned judge, while privileged state is not exposed to the policy.

Environment randomization.

To further broaden training experience within each environment, we randomize four complementary dimensions in Player-1-Gym: (1) Appearance: colors, lighting, and assets; (2) Camera: projection, placement, and initial orientation; (3) Scene: layouts, spawns, and task-specific configurations; and (4) Control: input-response gains for camera rotation, movement, driving, and steering where applicable. All four dimensions are jointly randomized during training where supported. Examples are provided in Figure 3(c). Appendix C further specifies the distributions and per-environment settings.

Multi-environment reinforcement learning.

We jointly optimize the SFT-initialized policy with PPO across randomized environments with different control demands, dynamics, and reward scales. To limit the effect of reward-scale differences on policy-update magnitudes, we apply per-environment advantage normalization to generalized advantage estimates (GAE):

A~i,j=Ai,j−μeσe2+ϵ,μe=∑(i,j)∈𝒮eAi,jNe,σe2=∑(i,j)∈𝒮e(Ai,j−μe)2Ne−1.\widetilde{A}_{i,j}=\frac{A_{i,j}-\mu_{e}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{e}^{2}+\epsilon}},\quad\mu_{e}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}A_{i,j}}{N_{e}},\quad\sigma_{e}^{2}=\frac{\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e}}(A_{i,j}-\mu_{e})^{2}}{N_{e}-1}. (1)

Here ii indexes turns and jj response tokens. For each environment ee, 𝒮e\mathcal{S}_{e} contains its response-token indices in the rollout batch, with Ne=|𝒮e|N_{e}=|\mathcal{S}_{e}|. We normalize each Ai,jA_{i,j} for (i,j)∈𝒮e(i,j)\in\mathcal{S}_{e} using the corresponding advantage mean μe\mu_{e} and sample variance σe2\sigma_{e}^{2}. Return-to-go targets accumulate rewards from subsequent turns, allowing later outcomes to inform earlier control decisions. Appendix D.2 further details reward construction, cross-turn credit, loss aggregation, and optimization.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Training setup.

We initialize Player-1-9B and Player-1-35B-A3B from their respective Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B backbones. Both undergo two epochs of SFT on the full demonstration dataset with action-balanced sampling. We then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) in the sixteen-environment Player-1-Gym suite. Both model sizes train on the full sixteen-environment suite with a budget of 200 RL steps. Each training step collects 256 episodes allocated equally across environments, with at most 50 interaction turns per episode. More training details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix D.

Evaluation.

Besides in-domain evaluation of sixteen Player-1-Gym environments, we construct two evaluation suites: MineDojo-300, comprising 300 tasks from the MineDojo (Fan et al., 2022) task collection in Minecraft, and ViZDoom-10, comprising ten maps from the twelve available maps in ViZDoom (Kempka et al., 2016). We also evaluate browser-game interaction on GameWorld (Ouyang et al., 2026), covering 170 tasks across 34 games. Our standardized evaluation protocols use 8 trials per MineDojo task, 50 per ViZDoom map, and 3 per GameWorld task. Appendix E details benchmark composition, metrics, and budgets.

We compare against game-specific models, including JARVIS-VLA (Li et al., 2025), NitroGen (Magne et al., 2026), Open-P2P (Yue et al., 2026), and GameWAM (Guo et al., 2026), as well as computer-use models, including UI-TARS-1.5-7B (ByteDance Seed, 2025) and our Qwen3.5 base models. We keep their native preprocessing and inference procedures across the benchmarks. We also compare the base models, our SFT-initialized models, and the final Player-1 models to separate the gains from SFT and those from synthetic experience.

4.2 Main Results

Task-directed control in Minecraft.

On MineDojo-300, SFT raises success from 9.21% to 10.54% for 9B and from 7.79% to 23.38% for 35B-A3B. Interactive learning raises 9B success to 38.33%, a large gain of 27.79 percentage points over SFT. The number of tasks completed in at least four of eight trials increases from 20 to 136, showing gains in both task coverage and repeatability.

Generalization beyond the RL training suite.

The same policy improves performance on external games. On ViZDoom-10, Player-1-9B increases scaled return from 0.4361 after SFT to 0.6922. Player-1-35B-A3B achieves an overall scaled return of 0.7236, surpassing GameWAM, the strongest external baseline at 0.3938, by 83.7%. On GameWorld’s 3×1703\times 170 episodes, progress rises from 31.43% to 34.45%. Together, these results show that control experience acquired in Player-1-Gym transfers to first-person shooting and distinct browser games, beyond the synthesized environments for RL. These gains support using synthetic experience to develop transferable control capabilities without reinforcement learning in each target game.

Case Example: Control in an Unseen Commercial Game.

We integrate Player-1 into commercial games using an observation–action loop with visual inputs and keyboard–mouse controls. Figure 4 shows an example sequence in Watch Dogs 2, a game unseen during both SFT and RL. Experience acquired during training enables the agent to reason and act across on-foot navigation, target approach, vehicle interaction, and driving scenarios.

5 Analysis

5.1 Learning Dynamics

In this section, we illustrate the learning dynamics of the SFT-initialized policies over RL steps. Figure 5(a,b) separates penalized episode returns from unpenalized game scores, with each metric averaged across sixteen environments.

Learning beyond SFT.

As shown in Figure 5(a,b), both mean episode return and mean game score rise across the RL training steps. Gains are largest early in training and become more gradual later. The 35B-A3B curve finishes slightly above the 9B curve on both measures. These trends indicate that learning from synthetic experience improves game control beyond SFT.

Effect of supervised initialization.

Figure 5(c) contrasts the displayed Base→\rightarrowRL and SFT→\rightarrowRL trajectories for 9B over 100 RL steps. SFT→\rightarrowRL rises from 17.67% to 51.67% Minecraft success, while Base→\rightarrowRL rises from 12.67% to 16.67%, leaving a 35.00-percentage-point gap at step 100.

Learning across environments.

Figure 6 breaks down episode returns across all sixteen training environments. Both models show broad net gains, but their learning trajectories vary across environments. For example, performance on simpler tasks such as 2D aiming improves rapidly and then levels off, whereas gains in 2D circuit driving emerge much later.

5.2 Environment Scaling

Expanding the training suite.

The scaling comparison allocates a fixed budget of 25,600 episodes over 100 RL steps across 2, 4, 8, or 16 environments, starting from the same Player-1-9B-SFT checkpoint. Each configuration uses 256 episodes per step, allocated equally across the environments. Appendix D.4 specifies the subsets and protocol.

5.3 Evolution of Action Composition

Figure 8 shows increased use of composite actions during RL. Across Player-1-9B’s in-suite validation trajectories, the share of turns with composite actions rises from 64.7% at the start of RL to 85.4% and 93.2% after 50 and 100 RL steps, respectively. This progressive increase occurs without an explicit reward for action composition, suggesting that task-driven RL reinforces coordinated inputs common to game control, such as aiming while firing or moving while adjusting the camera.

6 Conclusion

We presented Player-1, a post-training framework for learning game control beyond demonstrations through synthetic experience. Curated gameplay demonstrations initialize computer-use models in a shared game-control action space. Player-1-Gym then provides sixteen synthetic environments organized around shared control demands, with verifiable rewards and randomized observations and control dynamics for multi-environment RL. Evaluations on MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld demonstrate that learning from synthetic experience advances game-control capabilities beyond SFT, with gains that generalize beyond the RL training suite. Further analyses show improved transfer with larger training suites. Together, these findings establish synthetic experience as an effective resource for learning transferable game control without online training in each target game.

Appendix A Game-Control Interface

A.1 Coordinates and Composite Actions

Table 5 specifies the execution semantics of the actions introduced in Section 3.1. For an observation of width WW and height HH, normalized absolute positions and relative displacements map to pixels as

(x,y)↦(x​W/1000,y​H/1000),(Δ​x,Δ​y)↦(Δ​x​W/1000,Δ​y​H/1000).(x,y)\mapsto(xW/1000,yH/1000),\qquad(\Delta x,\Delta y)\mapsto(\Delta xW/1000,\Delta yH/1000).

The origin is the upper-left corner, and positive displacement points right and down. One movement uses either absolute or relative coordinates. A key cannot be both held and tapped in the same step, nor can one mouse button be both held and clicked.

A.2 Execution and Visual Feedback

Relative motion requests input displacement, not a universal camera angle. For per-pixel camera gain gg, requested yaw and pitch increments δ​ψ\delta\psi and δ​ϕ\delta\phi have magnitudes

|δ​ψ|=g​W​|Δ​x|/1000,|δ​ϕ|=g​H​|Δ​y|/1000,|\delta\psi|=gW|\Delta x|/1000,\qquad|\delta\phi|=gH|\Delta y|/1000,

before native camera limits; mouse displacement is not multiplied by action duration. The seven mouse-controlled 3D Player-1-Gym environments use a nominal gain g0=0.00196g_{0}=0.00196 radians per observation pixel by default. With Control randomization, the effective gain is g=g0​Lg=g_{0}L, where LL is defined in Appendix C.2. Observation geometry and camera constraints remain fixed within a checkpoint comparison. Benchmark-specific settings are given in Appendix E.

A.3 Observation and Interaction History

SFT, RL, and evaluation all use two recent visual–action turns and two earlier action-only turns. In the earlier action-only turns, screenshots are replaced by <image omitted>; reasoning in all retained historical turns is replaced by <thinking omitted>. The current screenshot and executed historical actions are retained.

Appendix B Gameplay Demonstrations: Construction and Annotation

B.1 Sources and Statistics

Both model sizes are trained with the collection in Figure 9: 6,044 trajectories and 295,097 turns from 2,544 source-qualified recording sessions and 172 games. We approximate the sampled control hours, which equal the turn count ×\times 200 ms, or 16.4 hours in total for the full annotated dataset.

Quality selection.

We automated validity, activity, and repetition checks that complement source-level and manual review of recording completeness, observation–action alignment, and sequence diversity. The collection contains 5,360 gameplay trajectories with a total of 268,000 turns and 684 in-game UI trajectories with a total of 27,097 turns.

Action statistics.

Figure 2(a) counts the distribution of each action across all samples in the dataset. Keyboard–mouse composites take precedence. Mouse-only turns are assigned by movement, click, hold, then scroll. Inputs per step count each key tap/hold and mouse operation separately, with wait as one no-op. Pointer-mode shares use all turns containing mouse_move, including keyboard–mouse composites.

B.2 Action Standardization

Temporal alignment.

For continuous gameplay, source timestamps define contiguous intervals of 150–250 ms, projected onto a 200-ms target grid using cumulative boundaries. Relative input is summed within each source interval. Keyboard presses shorter than 100 ms become taps, and longer presses become holds on overlapping target steps. Mouse presses lasting at most 300 ms become clicks. Each target summarizes compatible recorded inputs for concurrent execution within one control step.

UI trajectories also follow recorded operation boundaries. Clicks retain their recorded targets, key sequences expand into individual presses, drags use start and endpoint controls with an explicit release, and scroll gestures become directional steps. Execution uses the shared 200-ms action space. Sampled control hours use target execution duration, while UI trajectories retain their recorded, operation-dependent timing.

Spatial alignment.

Native relative-mouse input scales vary across data sources and recording setups. We therefore calibrate these inputs to pixel-equivalent displacements using freely moving GUI pointers from the same recording session. The mapping also applies to pointer-locked recordings. Camera response is defined in Appendix A.2. For native-input sums (rx,ry)(r_{x},r_{y}), coefficients (kx,ky)(k_{x},k_{y}), and logical recording size (Wm,Hm)(W_{m},H_{m}), the normalized target is

Δ​x=round⁡(1000​kx​rx/Wm),Δ​y=round⁡(1000​ky​ry/Hm).\Delta x=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{x}r_{x}/W_{m}),\qquad\Delta y=\operatorname{round}(1000k_{y}r_{y}/H_{m}).

Mouse-move Calibration.

In-house and D2E calibration uses GUI windows with stable focus and geometry, aligned timestamps, and no pointer clipping or recentering. For paired native input rir_{i} and pointer displacement pip_{i}, window and pooled session estimates are

ki=ri⊤​piri⊤​ri,k^=∑iri⊤​pi∑iri⊤​ri.k_{i}=\frac{r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}},\qquad\hat{k}=\frac{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}p_{i}}{\sum_{i}r_{i}^{\top}r_{i}}.

D2E uses window-equal estimates for a source-level coefficient; in-house coefficients are recording-specific. Pixel2Play uses per-axis Huber regression over at least two stable, non-overlapping two-second GUI blocks. Out-of-range projections are rejected rather than clipped to ensure the action quality. Table 6 lists the source mappings.

B.3 Goal and Reasoning Annotation

We use Gemini 3.8 Flash to build reusable profiles of rules, roles, inputs, and examples for each game in the trajectory, and check them for recorded-control coverage and action validity. It assigns goals from each profile, full-trajectory storyboard, and action timeline. The same game from different data sources should share the same assembled profile. For per-turn reasoning annotation, it re-uses the goal, fixed action target, and current and past frames.

Appendix C Player-1-Gym: Tasks, Rewards, and Randomization

C.1 Tasks and Verifiable Rewards

By primary task, the sixteen environments comprise aiming (2), combat (5), driving (4), navigation (4), and UI interaction (1). Tables 7 and 8 specify their tasks, score components, and API state fields. Interaction tests, score checks, and human review verify controls, observable transitions, and reward events against human-defined rules.

We designed the shared Three.js browser runtime to provide controllable resets, keyboard–mouse execution, screenshots, and rewards, with fixed-step simulation independent of inference latency. Each environment defines a cumulative score Se​(s)S_{e}(s) and supplies the increment re,t=Se​(st+1)−Se​(st)r_{e,t}=S_{e}(s_{t+1})-S_{e}(s_{t}) as reward. Reward computation and evaluation use privileged state, while the policy receives only screenshots and task/control text. Episodes only end on native completion or failure, or at the turn cap when the task is not completed under the limits.

C.2 Randomization and Sampling

Figure 10 shows individual and joint Appearance, Camera, and Scene variation. The parameters, distributions, and applicable environments for Appearance, Camera, Scene, and Control are specified in Table 9. Specifically, appearance preserves collision geometry and functional roles; Scene varies layouts, spawns, and subsequent entity generation, potentially changing task difficulty. Appearance and Camera are sampled at reset and fixed within each episode, with triangular modes at native values. Background lightness and saturation, ambient intensity, and key-light intensity share one sampled quantile, and linked asset components receive compatible color changes. Orthographic zoom is relative to the native view, including 2D platforming. Initial first-person point-of-view yaw/pitch is distinct from camera-rig pitch.

Control-response sampling.

Control varies input response independently of camera projection and scene configuration. For each supported response parameter kk, we independently sample

ce,k∼Tri(ae,k,1,be,k),ce,k(t)=ce,k(0)throughout the episode.c_{e,k}\sim\operatorname{Tri}(a_{e,k},1,b_{e,k}),\qquad c_{e,k}(t)=c_{e,k}(0)\quad\text{throughout the episode}. (2)

The control seed is independent of domain randomization. Separate parameter substreams set values at reset, unchanged through respawns. The narrower chasing, platforming, and jump ranges preserve pursuit-speed and traversal constraints. Collision rules, gravity, attack timing, control bindings, and reward definitions remain fixed. Table 10 specifies the training mixture.

Appendix D Post-Training Details

D.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

For supervised fine-tuning, both model sizes use token-level cross-entropy on the current turn’s reasoning and action, with the history in Appendix A.3.

Action-balanced sampling.

In human gameplay recordings, some actions occupy only a small fraction of playing time but are critical for game progress. For example, left mouse button inputs account for less than 1% of valid inputs in the original recordings, which are dominated by keyboard inputs and mouse movement. In addition to selecting and filtering demonstrations for action coverage during data curation, we use action-balanced sampling to strengthen supervision for these infrequent but important actions. We classify each turn by its current recorded action into overlapping pools: keyboard, mouse movement, click, hold, any mouse button, keyboard–mouse, movement–click, keyboard–click, and keyboard–movement–click. Keyboard includes held and tapped keys; keyboard–mouse includes any mouse input, including scrolling. Other contains the remaining turns, including wait and scroll-only actions. Each draw selects a pool proportionally to its weight (1 for each control pool; 0.1 for Other), then samples a turn uniformly with replacement.

D.2 Multi-Environment Reinforcement Learning

During RL, we use synchronous PPO with a dense critic initialized from Qwen3.5-9B for both actor sizes. Before actor updates begin, the critic undergoes five warmup iterations under the same environment configuration. Rollouts retain the observations, prompts, responses, masks, and behavior log probabilities used at generation, preserving the same conditioning during optimization.

Reward and cross-turn credit.

For turn tt in environment ee, we define the penalized step reward and undiscounted return-to-go as

r~e,t=re,t−pe,tinvalid−pe,tlength,Ge,t=∑u=tTr~e,u,\widetilde{r}_{e,t}=r_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t},\qquad G_{e,t}=\sum_{u=t}^{T}\widetilde{r}_{e,u}, (3)

where re,tr_{e,t} is the game-score increment (Appendix C.1) and TT the terminal turn. Training curves average episode returns Ge,1G_{e,1}. The penalties are

pe,tinvalid=𝟏​[invalid action],pe,tlength=min⁡{1, 0.005​max⁡(0,ntreason−64)},p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}=\mathbf{1}[\text{invalid action}],\qquad p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t}=\min\{1,\,0.005\max(0,n_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}}-64)\},

where ntreasonn_{t}^{\mathrm{reason}} counts generated reasoning/prose tokens. An invalid action executes the runtime’s wait fallback. We apply no additional terminal-failure penalty or task-wise reward rescaling. With γ=λ=1\gamma=\lambda=1, return targets are computed over complete trajectories, preserving cross-turn credit.

Advantage normalization and loss reduction.

We normalize advantages globally in GAE, then within environments using Equation (1), with Ne≥2N_{e}\geq 2 and ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}; critic return targets are unchanged. For minibatch ℬ\mathcal{B}, let 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} be turn ii’s nonempty response-token set selected by the loss mask. The clipped PPO loss averages within turns, then across turns:

ℒpolicy​(θ)=1|ℬ|​∑i∈ℬ1|𝒯i|​∑j∈𝒯iℓi,jPPO​(θ,A~i,j).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{policy}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}_{i}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{T}_{i}}\ell^{\mathrm{PPO}}_{i,j}(\theta;\widetilde{A}_{i,j}). (4)

The critic uses the same reduction. Normalization is token-weighted within environments, whereas losses weight turns equally. Each environment therefore contributes in proportion to its included turns.

D.3 Training Implementation

Table 10 summarizes the shared recipe for both model sizes. For each model size, the SFT stage uses 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs and takes approximately 24 hours, while a 200-step RL run uses 64 H200 GPUs and takes approximately 36 hours. Both durations include validation. Browser rollouts use a cluster-wide pool of 32 workers, each managing up to 16 isolated Playwright browser contexts, for a total capacity of 512 concurrent environments. Browser processes and contexts are reused across episodes to amortize startup costs.

D.4 Environment-Scaling Protocol

For Section 5.2, 9B policies start independently from the same SFT checkpoint, sharing the PPO, history, reward, and randomization settings in Table 10. Table 11 gives the suites and matched episode budgets, while interaction lengths and compute may vary within different episodes. Comparisons share Minecraft development tasks and trial seeds, with SFT as the zero-environment reference.

Appendix E Evaluation and Results

Table 12 lists the full panels and budgets. Methods share each panel’s tasks, trial seeds, and decision budgets while retaining model-specific preprocessing and inference schedules. Periodic evaluation during RL steps uses 100 Minecraft tasks with three trials each, ten ViZDoom maps with ten episodes each, and 170 GameWorld tasks with one trial each. Qwen3.5, Player-1-SFT, and final Player-1-9B are deployed with the history in Appendix A.3.

Evaluation cost.

Our full MineDojo-300, ViZDoom-10, and GameWorld protocols allocate up to 3.14 million agent decision turns per model. Our in-suite validation records average roughly 3,000 input tokens and 100 output tokens per turn, including visual context and generated reasoning. Using these observed lengths as a workload proxy, a full-budget evaluation would cost approximately USD$110,000 at GPT-6 Astra’s standard API rates of USD$10 and USD$50 per million input and output tokens, respectively, before caching discounts.11 1 https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-6-astra, accessed Sep 24, 2026. Actual costs depend on model-specific tokenization, reasoning, and episode lengths. Considering the estimated cost, our focus is mainly on representative released game-control and computer-use policies rather than proprietary API models.

E.1 Baseline Inference and Action Adapters

We deploy JARVIS-VLA with its action-token decoder and two history entries to predict one action per decision. UI-TARS-1.5-7B uses three previous screenshots, deterministic decoding, and a 400-token output limit. Its adapter maps pixel-coordinate actions to one benchmark interval, with drag and double-click unsupported. NitroGen aggregates an 18-action chunk into six benchmark decisions (three native actions per decision), refreshing the image after each chunk. GameWAM predicts 16 actions and executes eight before replanning, using its Minecraft checkpoint outside Doom and its ViZDoom checkpoint for Doom. Open-P2P uses visual-only conditioning and session-specific recurrent state. All temporal inference state is isolated between episodes.

Model inputs retain the released preprocessing for the best practice of each baseline: Minecraft is rendered at 864×480864\times 480. We resize the screenshots to 640×360640\times 360 for JARVIS-VLA and UI-TARS, 256×256256\times 256 for NitroGen, 224×224224\times 224 for GameWAM, and 192×192192\times 192 for Open-P2P. JARVIS-VLA and GameWAM retain their native degree-based Minecraft camera actions, while Open-P2P uses an adapter gain of 0.150.15 degrees per raw mouse pixel. Browser-game adapters project native actions onto per-game and per-role bindings. Benchmark action intervals remain fixed, so a native action chunk can span different simulated durations across benchmarks.

E.2 Player-1-Gym In-Suite Validation

In-suite validation uses the seeded panel in Table 12 with the training randomization settings. For an episode of TT turns in environment ee, the return is

Ge,1=∑t=1T(re,t−pe,tinvalid−pe,tlength).G_{e,1}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(r_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{invalid}}_{e,t}-p^{\mathrm{length}}_{e,t}\right).

Here re,t=Se​(st+1)−Se​(st)r_{e,t}=S_{e}(s_{t+1})-S_{e}(s_{t}) is the native game-score increment (Appendix C.1), and the invalid-action and length penalties are defined in Appendix D.2. We report mean episode return, averaging trials within each environment and then equally across the sixteen environments.

E.3 MineDojo-300

MineDojo-300 contains 200 Combat and 100 Harvest tasks from MineDojo, ported to MineStudio on Minecraft 1.16.5. World and task seeds are deterministically derived from each task and trial. Success is verified after initialization from inventory acquisition for Harvest tasks or target kills for Combat tasks. We average success over trials within each task, then equally over tasks. One decision advances a 50-ms simulator tick. Player-1’s camera adapter uses a nominal gain of 0.001960.00196 radians per observation pixel, subject to native constraints.

We also report Task coverage in Cm=∑i=1N𝟏[si≥m]C_{m}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}\geq m] for m∈{1,2,4}m\in\{1,2,4\}, where sis_{i} counts successes among eight trials for task ii. Entries Cm/NC_{m}/N, with N=300N=300, count tasks meeting each threshold. Overall success intervals use 100,000 percentile task-cluster bootstrap replicates, stratified by Combat and Harvest while retaining all eight trials per task and the panel’s category weights. The 95% intervals quantify within-panel task-sampling uncertainty. For all-zero outcomes, we report [-].

E.4 ViZDoom-10

Table 13 lists the ten selected maps, control categories, native rewards, and fixed return scales. ViZDoom 1.3.0 provides 640×480640\times 480 RGB observations. Each decision advances two simulator tics. Basic permits 150 decisions, Deathmatch 2,100, and the other maps 1,050, subject to earlier native termination. Player-1’s camera adapter uses 0.001960.00196 radians per observation pixel with native pitch constraints.

From raw return Rm,sR_{m,s} and map-specific scale cm>0c_{m}>0, we compute map, category (ℳc\mathcal{M}_{c}), and overall scaled returns:

Sm=1N​∑s=1NRm,scm,Sc=1|ℳc|​∑m∈ℳcSm,Soverall=110​∑m=110Sm.S_{m}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{s=1}^{N}\frac{R_{m,s}}{c_{m}},\qquad S_{c}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}_{c}|}\sum_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{c}}S_{m},\qquad S_{\mathrm{overall}}=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{m=1}^{10}S_{m}.

Evaluation uses N=50N=50 fixed seeds per map, with identical scales across models. The survival scale of 2,100 corresponds to the native time-reward budget, with death penalties retained. Observation geometry, timing, and camera constraints are matched within each backbone.

E.5 GameWorld

GameWorld includes 170 tasks across 34 diverse browser games. We evaluate our model for three trials with seeds 0, 1, and 2 (Table 12). The policy receives screenshots, rules, and instructions, while evaluator state is hidden. Action duration, observation geometry, and admissible controls follow each game’s configuration, and multi-role games keep separate histories. Success is the fraction of trials reporting completion, while progress is the achieved fraction from its initial value to its target, clipped to [0,1][0,1]. The evaluator averages objectives and retains the best task progress reached. Reported success and progress average trials within each task, then equally across tasks.
